articles.title: Why the Same 0.01 mm Part Measures Differently in Two Buildings
articles.excerpt: A 20 µm tolerance band is not a property of the metal. Temperature, probe contact, clamping and datum choice each take a slice of it — and the slices add up faster than most drawings assume. A bracket…
articles.body: A 20 µm tolerance band is not a property of the metal. Temperature, probe contact, clamping and datum choice each take a slice of it — and the slices add up faster than most drawings assume. A bracket comes off the machine at 09:40. The supplier's CMM says the bore spacing is 99.996 mm. The part flies to the customer, and their incoming inspection reports 100.009 mm. Both machines carry a valid calibration certificate. Both operators followed the drawing. The tolerance is ±0.01 mm, so one of them accepted the part and the other rejected it. In most of these disputes nobody is lying and nobody is incompetent. The two measurements are answering slightly different questions, because a ±0.01 mm callout is only meaningful together with a temperature, a fixturing state and a datum scheme.

articles.title: Data Engineer Resume: How to Show Scale, Reliability, Cost
articles.excerpt: Nobody notices a pipeline that runs on time. Your resume's job is to make that invisible work visible. Short answer: a strong data engineer resume answers three questions in every bullet — how much da…
articles.body: Nobody notices a pipeline that runs on time. Your resume's job is to make that invisible work visible. Short answer: a strong data engineer resume answers three questions in every bullet — how much data , how reliably , and at what cost . A list of tools (Spark, Airflow, dbt, Snowflake, Kafka) answers none of them. Hiring managers for data roles assume you've touched the stack; what they can't assume is the scale you ran it at or what broke on your watch. Why data engineer resumes read the same Most data engineering work is maintenance of things that are supposed to be boring. When it succeeds, nothing happens. So the easy resume to write is a stack list plus "built and maintained ETL pipelines" — and because everyone writes that line, it carries no information.

articles.body: How much faster does air get replaced with two windows open instead of one? With only the exhaust fan running, where does air stagnate? I made a page that computes this for a two-bedroom apartment and colors how old the air is in each spot (the age of air) . No libraries. https://sishiya.github.io/manabi-lab/air-flow/?lang=en The calculation has three stages: How much air the whole home exchanges (ventilation network) How air moves through the home (2D flow) How long ago the air at each spot came in from outside (age of air) This post covers the equations for each and where I got stuck in stage 3. 1.

articles.title: Node.js AI Image Generation: Decode Errors in Compatible Object Storage
articles.excerpt: Short answer: S3-compatible object storage is a good home for AI-generated images when a worker uploads the PNG buffer as binary, verifies the stored metadata before its database commit, and serves th…
articles.body: Short answer: S3-compatible object storage is a good home for AI-generated images when a worker uploads the PNG buffer as binary, verifies the stored metadata before its database commit, and serves the result with a presigned link instead of a permanent public URL. A malformed base64 decode error is usually an ownership mistake at an interface. A PNG already has bytes; turning those bytes into text for a queue, then decoding them again before upload, creates room for a data-URL prefix, missing padding, or a second decode. Decode at the documented generation boundary once, validate the bytes, and keep the rest of the path binary. Small rule. Large consequence. What signal says a Node.js generated PNG needs an object-storage runbook?

articles.title: Why Multi-Agent Swarms Keep Failing in Production (and a 24-Point Reliability Matrix)
articles.excerpt: Most multi-agent demos built in an IDE work smoothly for 10 turns. But the moment you deploy topologies to production against live databases, asynchronous queues, and noisy inputs, they hit consistent…
articles.body: Most multi-agent demos built in an IDE work smoothly for 10 turns. But the moment you deploy topologies to production against live databases, asynchronous queues, and noisy inputs, they hit consistent failure modes that prompt engineering alone cannot fix. After evaluating dozens of agent failure traces across production runtimes, the breakdown almost never comes from poor base-model reasoning. It comes from absent distributed systems engineering and missing runtime guardrails. Here are the four primary failure modes we see in the wild—and how to harden your architecture against them. 1. Unconstrained ReAct Loops ("Death Loops") The Breakdown: An agent encounters a transient HTTP 503 or a malformed API payload.

articles.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community
articles.excerpt: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall.
articles.body: Dear NASA Science Community, NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions. We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.

articles.title: Sci-fi legend Alan Dean Foster on his new futuristic adventure 'Lost On Paradise': 'It's paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up' (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise.'
articles.body: Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, " Lost on Paradise ", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week. Foster famously ghost-wrote the first " Star Wars " novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades.
